title: Frobenius twist and root datum of a split reductive group
statement: Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure] of characteristic $p>0$. Let $G$ be a reductive $F$-group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme], meaning smooth, connected, affine and of finite type with no nontrivial smooth connected normal unipotent subgroup. Unipotent means unipotent matrices at geometric points in a faithful representation. Fix a split maximal torus $T\subseteq G$, and use its reduced root datum $(M,\Phi,M^\vee,\Phi^\vee)$ as in [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure], with $M=X^*(T)=\operatorname{Hom}_{F\text{-groups}}(T,\mathbf G_m)$ and $\mathbf G_m(A)=A^\times$. Put $\sigma(a)=a^p$, $C=F[G]$, $G^{(p)}=\operatorname{Spec}(C\otimes_{F,\sigma}F)$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum] with the base-changed group operations, and let $T^{(p)}\subseteq G^{(p)}$ be the base change of $T$. Then $G^{(p)}$ is reductive and $T^{(p)}$ is a split maximal torus. Base change of characters gives an isomorphism $\iota:M\xrightarrow{\sim}X^*(T^{(p)})$, $\chi\mapsto\chi^{(p)}$, where the base change of $\mathbf G_m$ is identified with $\mathbf G_m$ by its Laurent coordinate. Together with the base change of cocharacters, $\iota$ identifies the full reduced root data: roots correspond by $\alpha\mapsto\alpha^{(p)}$ and their coroots by $\alpha^\vee\mapsto(\alpha^\vee)^{(p)}$, preserving the integer pairing. The relative Frobenius $F_{G/F}:G\to G^{(p)}$, whose coordinate map is $b\otimes c\mapsto cb^p$, is a surjective faithfully flat group homomorphism with finite scheme-theoretic kernel; finite means finite-dimensional coordinate algebra and faithfully flat means extension of scalars is exact and detects zero modules. It maps $T$ into $T^{(p)}$, and $\chi^{(p)}\circ F_{G/F}|_T=p\chi$ for every $\chi\in M$. The torus and trivial-group cases are included.

source.place: 2.25--2.29, printed pp.47--49 (twist, functoriality, group homomorphism and faithfully flat Frobenius isogeny); proof of 23.27, p.493 (root data unchanged by base field extension), applied to the field automorphism sigma; 12.9 and 21.11 (characters and canonical root datum).

proof.text: The field map $\sigma$ is bijective: $a^p=b^p$ implies $(a-b)^p=0$, hence $a=b$ in a field; every $c\in F$ has a $p$th root since $X^p-c$ has a root in $F$. For any commutative $F$-algebra $A$, set $A^\sigma=A\otimes_{F,\sigma}F$. The tensor balancing relation is $(\lambda a)\otimes c=a\otimes\sigma(\lambda)c$. Consequently $j_A:a\mapsto a\otimes1$ is a bijective ring map, with inverse $a\otimes c\mapsto\sigma^{-1}(c)a$; it is $\sigma$-semilinear. The two inverse identities follow by substituting the balancing relation. For every $F$-algebra map $f:A\to D$, $f^\sigma j_A=j_D f$. Twisting by $\sigma^{-1}$ reverses this operation, also on maps. The maps $j$ identify the underlying spectra, although they need not be $F$-morphisms. Tensoring the multiplication, identity and inverse diagrams therefore gives the specified group structure on $G^{(p)}$.

source.place: 2.24--2.28, printed pp.46--49; the inverse for an automorphism of the base field is written explicitly.

proof.text: This operation preserves affineness, finite type and connectedness: the underlying rings and spectra are isomorphic by step 1, and a finite algebra generating family is carried to a finite generating family. It also preserves smoothness, directly from [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms]. A finite presentation is carried to the presentation with every coefficient acted on by $\sigma$, and twisting back recovers the original presentation. For a first-order affine thickening and a lifting problem over the twisted field structure, twist the entire diagram by $\sigma^{-1}$. Its ideal still has square zero. Formal smoothness of the original scheme gives a lift; twisting the lift forward solves the original diagram, with the same restriction. This proves preservation of formal smoothness and local finite presentation, and hence smoothness. Apply this to $G$ and, when needed, to its smooth closed subgroups.

source.place: 2.29, printed pp.48--49, first part of its proof; smoothness under the field automorphism is checked using the infinitesimal definition.

proof.text: Twisting and its inverse carry closed subgroup diagrams and their conjugation diagrams to closed subgroup diagrams and conjugation diagrams; thus inclusions and normality are preserved and reflected. A faithful matrix representation twists to a faithful matrix representation, since twisting the defining coordinate maps is invertible. The matrix identity $(u-I)^n=0$ twists to the identical matrix identity: addition, multiplication and $I$ are preserved. The equivalence on test algebras therefore preserves and reflects unipotence on all geometric points. If $G^{(p)}$ had a nontrivial smooth connected normal unipotent subgroup, its inverse twist would have all these properties in $G$, contradicting reductivity. Thus $G^{(p)}$ is reductive. Twisting a splitting $T\simeq\mathbf G_m^r$ gives $T^{(p)}\simeq\mathbf G_m^r$, since the Laurent-coordinate group operations have integer coefficients. Any larger torus in $G^{(p)}$ inverse-twists to a larger torus in $G$. Hence $T^{(p)}$ is split and maximal.

source.place: 2.26--2.29, printed pp.47--49; reductivity and maximality checked using the invertible change of field structure, as in the base-change observation in 23.27, p.493.

proof.text:
Twist the maps $\chi:T	o\mathbf G_m$ and $
u:\mathbf G_m	o T$. The Laurent-coordinate identification $(F[z,z^{-1}])^\sigma\simeq F[z,z^{-1}]$ sends $z\otimes1$ to $z$ and $1\otimes c$ to $c$. Step 1 and its inverse therefore give inverse bijections on characters and on cocharacters; they are group homomorphisms because pointwise multiplication of maps is preserved. These give the asserted lattice isomorphisms. If $\chi
u$ has coordinate $z\mapsto z^n$, its twist still has coordinate $z\mapsto z^n$, including $n<0$. Thus $\langle\chi^{(p)},
u^{(p)}angle=\langle\chi,
uangle$. This is the integer pairing specified in [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure], so the full character and cocharacter lattices, including central torus directions, are retained.

source.place: 12.9(a), printed pp.233--234; 21a and 21.12, pp.424--430; the character/cocharacter maps and pairing are calculated on Laurent coordinates.

proof.text: Use the tangent-space and character-weight description in [lem-sfb-reductive-rank-one-reflections]. Twisting identifies tangent vectors by applying step 1 to $F[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^2)$: the coefficient map $a+\varepsilon b\mapsto\sigma(a)+\varepsilon\sigma(b)$ respects addition, multiplication and evaluation at $\varepsilon=0$. In the kernel of $G(F[\varepsilon])\to G(F)$ this gives a bijective $\sigma$-semilinear map $J:\mathfrak g\to\mathfrak g^{(p)}$. Addition is given by multiplication of tangent points, and scalar multiplication by substitution $\varepsilon\mapsto c\varepsilon$, so $J$ is indeed semilinear. Differentiating conjugation amounts to evaluating that same conjugation diagram on dual numbers; its twist is the conjugation diagram for $T^{(p)}$ in $G^{(p)}$. Thus twisting the weight equation $t\cdot v=\alpha(t)v$, as an identity on test algebras, gives $t'\cdot J(v)=\alpha^{(p)}(t')J(v)$. The inverse twist gives the converse. The direct sum of weight spaces is consequently carried to the direct sum of the corresponding twisted weight spaces. Nonzero spaces and nonzero characters are preserved. The nonzero weights, hence the roots, correspond exactly by $\alpha\mapsto\alpha^{(p)}$.

source.place: 21.1--21.2, printed pp.424--425; 23.27, p.493, invariance of the root datum from its definition; tangent and weight comparison written out on dual numbers.

proof.text:
To identify coroots, use the rank-one centralizer and uniqueness assertions of [lem-sfb-reductive-rank-one-reflections], rather than differentials of characters. Twisting identifies $\ker\alpha$ with $\ker\alpha^{(p)}$ and preserves inclusions of tori in both directions, so it identifies their largest subtori $T_\alpha$ and $T_{\alpha^{(p)}}$. The centralizer equations $gt=tg$ on every test algebra twist to the same equations. Hence it identifies $(G_\alpha)^{(p)}$ with $(G^{(p)})_{\alpha^{(p)}}$ and also identifies their torus normalizers, their $F$-points and their quotients by the tori. The unique nonidentity element of the rank-one Weyl group therefore corresponds to the unique nonidentity element for the twisted root. Conjugation and character composition commute with twisting, giving $s_{\alpha^{(p)}}(x^{(p)})=(s_\alpha x)^{(p)}$. Apply the character-lattice isomorphism to $s_\alpha x=x-\langle x,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha$ and use step 4 to obtain
$$s_{\alpha^{(p)}}(x^{(p)})=x^{(p)}-\langle x^{(p)},(\alpha^\vee)^{(p)}\rangle\alpha^{(p)}.$$
Since every character is $x^{(p)}$, the cited uniqueness of the cocharacter in this reflection identity shows $(\alpha^{(p)})^\vee=(\alpha^\vee)^{(p)}$. Together with steps 4--5 this proves identification of the full reduced root data in every characteristic.

source.place: Theorem 21.11(d)--(e), printed pp.429--430, and proof of 23.27, p.493; coroots characterized by the unique rank-one reflection.

proof.text:
Put $B=C\otimes_{F,\sigma}F$. Define $\varphi:B\to C$ by $b\otimes c\mapsto cb^p$. The tensor universal property makes this an $F$-algebra map: additivity is $(b+d)^p=b^p+d^p$, and the balancing relation maps to $c(\lambda b)^p=\lambda^pcb^p$. By [lem-sfb-affine-group-coordinate-hopf], $C$ has the Hopf maps induced by the group operations. On $B$ use their scalar extensions. For $\Delta(b)=\sum_i b_i'\otimes b_i''$ the required compatibility is
$$\Delta(\varphi(b\otimes c))=c\sum_i(b_i')^p\otimes(b_i'')^p=(\varphi\otimes\varphi)\Delta_B(b\otimes c).$$
The counit and antipode compatibilities are $\epsilon(cb^p)=c\epsilon(b)^p$ and $S(cb^p)=cS(b)^p$. All are identities on pure tensors and hence on $B$. The Hopf-spectrum functor [lem-sfb-hopf-spectrum-functor] makes $\operatorname{Spec}\varphi$ a group homomorphism. Its displayed coordinate map is exactly that of $F_{G/F}$.

source.place: 2.24 and 2.27--2.28, printed pp.46--49; Proposition 3.6 and Corollary 3.7, pp.66--67.

proof.text: Apply [sbc-lem-smooth-geometrically-reduced] to the smooth structure morphism $G\to\operatorname{Spec}F$: its single fibre $G$ is reduced. Then [lem-weil-pbc-affine-scheme-reduced-iff] makes $C$ a reduced ring. Every $u=\sum_i b_i\otimes c_i\in B$ has the form $d\otimes1$ with $d=\sum_i\sigma^{-1}(c_i)b_i$, by the balancing relation of step 1. If $\varphi(u)=0$, then $d^p=0$, so reducedness gives $d=0$ and hence $u=0$. Thus $\varphi$ is injective. By [lem-pc-affine-finite-type-algebra], $C$ is finitely generated over $F$. If $z_1,\ldots,z_N$ generate $C$, then $z_1\otimes1,\ldots,z_N\otimes1$ generate $B$ over its right-hand copy of $F$; twisting a polynomial expression for $b$ simply acts on its coefficients by $\sigma$. Both Hopf algebras therefore meet the finite-generation hypothesis used next.

source.place: 2.29, printed pp.48--49, reducedness and dominance; Stacks Tags 056T (varieties, lemma-smooth-geometrically-normal), 01J2 (schemes, lemma-affine-reduced), and 01T2 (morphisms, lemma-locally-finite-type-characterize).

proof.text: The map $\varphi:B\to C$ is an injective homomorphism of finitely generated commutative Hopf $F$-algebras by steps 7--8. Apply [lem-sfb-hopf-subalgebra-faithfully-flat] with source $B$ and target $C$. It says exactly that extension of scalars along $\varphi$ is exact and detects zero modules, proving faithful flatness in the stated exactness-and-detection sense. For surjectivity on spectra no additional group-image theorem is needed: $\varphi\circ j_C$ is the absolute Frobenius $d\mapsto d^p$. Its inverse-image map on prime ideals is the identity, since $d^p\in\mathfrak p$ if and only if $d\in\mathfrak p$. Since $j_C$ is a ring isomorphism, $\operatorname{Spec}\varphi$ is a bijection on underlying points, in particular surjective.

source.place: Theorem 3.31, printed pp.73--74; 2.25--2.29, pp.47--49, for absolute Frobenius on points and faithful flatness of relative Frobenius.

proof.text:
The scheme-theoretic kernel is the fibre over the identity, with coordinate algebra $D=C\otimes_{B,\epsilon_B}F$. Let $\bar z_i$ be the images of the algebra generators from step 8. They generate $D$ as an $F$-algebra. In this tensor product,
$$\bar z_i^p=\varphi(z_i\otimes1)\otimes1=1\otimes\epsilon_B(z_i\otimes1)=\epsilon(z_i)^p.$$
Thus reducing powers of each $\bar z_i$ shows that the monomials $\prod_i\bar z_i^{e_i}$, $0\leq e_i<p$, span $D$ over $F$. There are at most $p^N$ such monomials. Hence $D$ is finite-dimensional and the kernel is finite. This calculation imposes no reducedness on the kernel, and applies also when $N=0$, with the empty monomial equal to $1$.

source.place: 2.24--2.29, printed pp.46--49; explicit finite-coordinate calculation for the Frobenius kernel.

proof.text: For any closed subgroup $H\subseteq G$, with coordinate quotient $C\to C_H$, taking $p$th powers commutes with the quotient map. Thus the Frobenius square for $H\to G$ commutes on pure tensors and $F_{G/F}$ maps $H$ into $H^{(p)}$. In particular it maps $T$ into $T^{(p)}$. If $u_\chi\in F[T]^\times$ is the invertible coordinate function of a character $\chi$, its twisted character has coordinate function $u_\chi\otimes1$. Pulling back by $F_{T/F}$ sends this to $u_\chi^p$, the coordinate function of $p\chi$. Therefore $\chi^{(p)}\circ F_{G/F}|_T=p\chi$. For a torus the root set is empty and steps 4 and 7--10 still apply; for $G=1$ the lattices and root sets are zero, $C=B=D=F$, and the homomorphism is the identity. These verify the stated edge cases.

source.place: 2.27(a), printed p.48, functoriality; Laurent-coordinate calculation of the torus restriction, with the empty-root and trivial-group cases.

The statement matches both, and I tested it on the torus case (kernel μ_p^r, nonreduced, dim p^r, χ^(p)∘F=pχ), on G=1, and on SL_2 coroots. Step by step: well-definedness of φ on the balancing relation and the inverse of j_A both hold. Smoothness transfers through the σ^{-1}-twisted lifting problem, and reductivity, unipotence and maximality transfer by the invertible twist. The twist keeps z↦z^n for n<0. On dual numbers it gives a σ-semilinear tangent map that respects weights. The coroot follows from rank-one-reflections' uniqueness clause, which is in its statement. The Hopf compatibilities hold because Δ(b)^p=Σ(b')^p⊗(b'')^p in characteristic p. φ is injective because C is reduced (smooth ⇒ reduced fibre G, then affine-reduced-iff). Faithful flatness comes from hopf-subalgebra-faithfully-flat with all its hypotheses met. Spec φ is bijective because φ∘j_C is absolute Frobenius. The kernel C⊗_{B,ε}F is spanned by at most p^N monomials since z̄_i^p=ε(z_i)^p. The torus pullback is u_χ↦u_χ^p. I found no duplicate in a search for Frobenius twist and relative Frobenius over the DAG; the nearest nodes are affine-group-frobenius-smooth-image, frobenius-twist-geometric-integrality, rank-one-frobenius-extension, isogeny-torus-conjugacy and trf 0CCD, and none states this item. No SGA. I accept the three tool uses (smooth-geometrically-reduced, affine-reduced-iff, affine-finite-type-algebra) as generic dictionaries. Its proof uses the canonical coroots of rank-one-reflections, and step 6 identifies exactly those. Rewording borel-pair-structure would make the convention explicit. No files changed.
